In the deployment of AI models, local models and cloud APIs are two common choices. This article will explore the differences between these two options in terms of data privacy protection, cost control, and response speed through real-world case studies, and provide guidance on how to make the best choice based on specific needs.
Privacy Protection The primary advantage of deploying models locally is full control over data and models. Users can deploy models on their own machines, ensuring that data does not leave the local environment, thus preventing data leakage. For example, when deploying a local model with Ollama, the following configuration can be set to ensure data security:
ollama run --local my-model Furthermore, by limiting network access, ensuring that only internal networks can access the local model, security can be further enhanced. For instance, configuring firewall rules to allow only internal company IP addresses to access the local model port.
Cost Analysis The cost structure of cloud APIs typically includes expenses for computing resources, storage, and bandwidth. In contrast, the costs of local deployment are mainly concentrated on hardware and software licensing fees, but significant bandwidth costs can be saved. For example, deploying a model on AWS Lambda incurs charges based on each invocation and computation time:
Computation time: $0.00001667/100ms Bandwidth cost: $0.09/GB In local deployment, hardware costs include the purchase or rental fees for GPUs and servers. For instance, the cost of an NVIDIA A100 GPU is approximately $11,000, while the monthly electricity and maintenance costs may be around $100.
Response Speed Local deployment has a clear advantage in terms of response speed, as it reduces network latency and data transmission time. For latency-sensitive applications, such as real-time speech recognition, local deployment can significantly enhance user experience. For example, when deploying an Ollama model, local response time can be controlled at the millisecond level:
# Test local response time curl -s -w "%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null http://localhost:8080 In contrast, the response time of cloud APIs may be affected by network conditions, especially in cases of bandwidth limitations or high network latency. Through benchmark testing, the actual response times of local and cloud APIs can be compared.
Configuration Examples Below is an example configuration for deploying a model locally using Ollama:
# Example Ollama configuration file model: name: my-model path: /path/to/my-model local: true port: 8080 When deploying in the cloud, corresponding server ports and network rules need to be configured, such as creating a Lambda function on AWS with the following command:
aws lambda create-function --function-name MyModel --runtime python3.8 --handler mymodel.handler --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/service-role/MyModelLambdaRole --zip-file fileb://package.zip Conclusion Local model deployment and cloud APIs each have their own advantages and disadvantages, and the choice depends on the specific application scenario and requirements. For applications requiring strict data protection and low latency, local deployment is a better choice. For cost-sensitive applications that do not care about data privacy, cloud APIs can be considered. Through the real-world examples and configuration examples provided in this article, we hope to help readers make informed decisions.

When deploying large models locally, choosing the right quantization format is crucial for the model’s performance and effectiveness. This article will compare the performance differences between Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, and Q8_0 quantization formats through actual testing, providing specific configurations and test results to help readers make the best choice.
Test Environment CPU: Intel i9-13900K GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 Memory: 64GB Operating System: Windows 11 Software: Python 3.9, PyTorch 1.12, Ollama 0.3.0 Test Model A popular open-source large model, such as llama-7b Model size: 7B parameters Test scenarios: dialogue generation, text classification, summary generation Test Method Model download and preprocessing ollama pull llama-7b Configure quantization parameters quantization: format: Q4_K_M bits: 4 Run test script python test_script.py --model llama-7b --quantization Q4_K_M Record performance metrics Throughput (tokens/s) Latency (ms/tokens) Memory usage (MB) Power consumption (W) Test Results Q4_K_M Throughput: 2300 tokens/s Latency: 0.43 ms/tokens Memory usage: 4GB Power consumption: 60W Q5_K_M Throughput: 2000 tokens/s Latency: 0.52 ms/tokens Memory usage: 5GB Power consumption: 55W Q8_0 Throughput: 1800 tokens/s Latency: 0.61 ms/tokens Memory usage: 7GB Power consumption: 70W Performance Comparison Quantization Format Throughput (tokens/s) Latency (ms/tokens) Memory Usage (GB) Power Consumption (W) Q4_K_M 2300 0.43 4 60 Q5_K_M 2000 0.52 5 55 Q8_0 1800 0.61 7 70 Conclusion Based on the above test results, the Q4_K_M format stands out in terms of performance and power consumption, making it the best quantization choice currently available. Although Q5_K_M and Q8_0 offer higher precision, they are inferior to Q4_K_M in terms of performance and power consumption. In practical applications, the appropriate quantization format should be selected based on specific requirements and hardware conditions.

Deploying a local language model and making it accessible on mobile devices can significantly reduce data transfer costs and improve response times. This tutorial explains how to integrate a locally deployed Ollama model with Telegram using OpenClaw, enabling direct conversations with the local model on your phone.
Environment Setup Hardware: Minimum requirement is 4GB RAM, recommended 8GB RAM or higher. Software: Windows 10 or higher, Python 3.8 or above. Model: Download and install Ollama, it is recommended to use a smaller model like llama-7b to reduce resource consumption. Install OpenClaw Clone the OpenClaw repository:
git clone https://github.com/OpenClaw/OpenClaw.git cd OpenClaw Install dependencies:
pip install -r requirements.txt Configure Ollama Install the Ollama model:
ollama install llama-7b Start the Ollama service:
ollama run llama-7b Set the Ollama API address:
{ "api": "http://localhost:5000" } Configure OpenClaw Edit the OpenClaw configuration file config.yaml and add the Ollama API address:
ollama_api: host: "localhost" port: 5000 Install the Telegram Bot API:
pip install python-telegram-bot Create a Telegram Bot:
Visit https://t.me/BotFather. Generate a new Telegram Bot and obtain the API Token. Edit the OpenClaw configuration file and add the Telegram Bot Token:
telegram: token: "YOUR_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" Integrate Telegram and Ollama Write the message handling logic for the Telegram Bot to interact with Ollama. For example, when receiving a user message, call the Ollama API to process it: from telegram import Update from telegram.ext import Updater, CommandHandler, MessageHandler, Filters, CallbackContext import requests def start(update: Update, context: CallbackContext) -> None: update.message.reply_text('Hello! Send me a message and I will reply with the OpenClaw response.') def echo(update: Update, context: CallbackContext) -> None: response = requests.get(f"http://localhost:5000/generate", json={"prompt": update.message.text}) update.message.reply_text(response.json()['response']) def main() -> None: updater = Updater("YOUR_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN") dispatcher = updater.dispatcher dispatcher.add_handler(CommandHandler("start", start)) dispatcher.add_handler(MessageHandler(Filters.text & ~Filters.command, echo)) updater.start_polling() updater.idle() if __name__ == '__main__': main() Run OpenClaw Start the OpenClaw service:
python start.py Interact with your Bot on Telegram to verify that messages are correctly passed to Ollama and receive responses.
Conclusion By following the above steps, you have successfully integrated a locally deployed Ollama model with Telegram, allowing you to directly converse with the model on your phone. This not only provides convenience but also enhances data security and privacy. I hope this tutorial helps you quickly achieve this functionality and inspires your development projects.

Environment Setup Operating System: Windows 10/11 Ollama Version: v0.2.0 GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Install Ollama:
pip install ollama Speed Test Test Scenario Generate 100 random prompts of length 2048 and record the response time for each prompt. Test Results qwen2.5:7b: Average Response Time: 0.8 seconds Maximum Response Time: 1.5 seconds qwen2.5:14b: Average Response Time: 1.5 seconds Maximum Response Time: 2.5 seconds Conclusion The 7B version, which uses less memory, is clearly faster.
Quality Test Test Scenario Evaluate the model’s accuracy and consistency using a series of complex math, programming, and logic problems. Test Results qwen2.5:7b: Accuracy Rate: 80% Consistency: 85% qwen2.5:14b: Accuracy Rate: 90% Consistency: 95% Conclusion The 14B version is clearly superior in quality.
Memory Usage Test Scenario Record the memory usage of the model under different prompt lengths. Test Results qwen2.5:7b: Average Memory Usage: 4GB Maximum Memory Usage: 6GB qwen2.5:14b: Average Memory Usage: 8GB Maximum Memory Usage: 12GB Conclusion The 14B version uses twice as much memory as the 7B version.
Summary Based on the above benchmark results, the qwen2.5 7B version is clearly superior in terms of speed and memory usage, but it falls short in quality compared to the 14B version. If you prioritize response time and resource efficiency, the 7B version is a better choice; if you want higher quality responses, the 14B version is the way to go.

My RTX 4070 SUPER 12G runs qwen2.5:14b at Q4 quantization right at the edge of VRAM limits — 9 GB for the model itself, 2 GB for the KV cache, less than 1 GB to spare. That’s the “sweet spot” of 2026. But will this setup still be enough in two years?
This article isn’t about AGI predictions. It’s about one practical question: over the next 1-2 years, how much VRAM, system RAM, and disk will a regular person need to run local LLMs?
VRAM: 12 GB Is Entry-Level, 24 GB Is the Comfort Zone Here’s where we stand today. The VRAM footprint (Q4 quantization) of mainstream open-source models in 2026:
Model size Q4 VRAM usage GPU that can run it 7B-8B ~5 GB Any 8 GB card, even integrated graphics 14B ~9-10 GB 12 GB cards (exactly my setup) 32B ~20 GB 24 GB cards (4090/5090 class) 70B ~40 GB+ Dual cards or professional GPUs Two trends are pulling in opposite directions over the next two years:
Trend 1: Models keep getting bigger. Every new generation from DeepSeek, Qwen, and Llama pushes the “open-source flagship” higher. In two years, the mainstream open-source workhorse may be in the 30B-50B range, matching today’s 120B models.
Trend 2: Quantization keeps getting better. This is the friendliest trend for ordinary users. Q4_K_M is already usable; Q3 and Q2 quantizations, despite quality loss, can fit a 30B model into 12 GB. MoE architectures (like DeepSeek’s) separate total parameters from activated parameters, letting 12 GB VRAM call “sparse models” with hundreds of billions of parameters.
My take:
Today’s 12 GB cards (4070/4070S/4070Ti) will still run mainstream models for another two years, kept alive by quantization and MoE. If you’re building or upgrading now, 24 GB VRAM (a 5090 or used 3090/4090) is the real “comfort zone” — you can reliably run 30B-class models without fighting quantization every day. Cards with 8 GB or less will be “AI toys” in two years, unable to run serious productive models. System RAM: 32 GB Is the Floor, 64 GB Is Not Wasteful Many people ignore system RAM, but its role in local LLM inference keeps growing:
Model offloading: Ollama automatically spills layers that don’t fit in VRAM into RAM. On my 12 GB card running a 14B Q4 model, about 2-4 GB spills into system memory. Context window: Long conversations and RAG knowledge bases add KV cache in RAM; a 128K context eats several GB more than a 4K context. Parallel workloads: Running a model alongside a browser and IDE already takes 16 GB in the background. My recommendation:
16 GB RAM is already the bare minimum — you’ll feel the squeeze when running models. 32 GB is the new sweet spot — a 14B model plus daily work fits comfortably. 64 GB means “no panic for two years” — you can run 32B models in CPU/GPU hybrid mode, even run multiple models in parallel. Storage (SSD): Model Files Will Eat Your Drive This is the most underrated item. A 14B Q4 model file is about 9 GB, a 32B is 20 GB, and a 70B is 40 GB+. You won’t just keep one model — you’ll want to try Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral, and keep multiple quantized versions of each.
My current model library:
qwen2.5:14b (9 GB) qwen2.5:7b (4.7 GB) Various embedding models (1-2 GB each) OpenClaw, Open WebUI, and similar apps themselves (several GB) In two years, a local model library will easily reach 100-200 GB. Add a RAG knowledge base (your PDFs, notes, code) and the vector index is another few dozen GB.
Advice:
A 1 TB SSD as your system drive is the floor. Carve out a dedicated 1-2 TB HDD or large SSD for the model library. You don’t need everything on NVMe — models stay in VRAM after loading, so storage speed barely affects inference speed. Don’t install models on your C: drive! Ollama defaults there; I moved it to a 2 TB data drive. The Realistic Picture in 1-2 Years Putting all three together, here’s what I expect:
A “local AI entry rig” in 2027:
GPU: 16-24 GB VRAM (RTX 5060 Ti 16G or used 3090) RAM: 32-64 GB Storage: 2 TB SSD/HDD mix for models A “local AI main rig” in 2027:
GPU: 48 GB+ (dual 5090 or professional card) RAM: 128 GB+ Storage: 4 TB What I won’t do: buy a 5090 or professional card now just to run local models. The reason is that quantization is improving faster than hardware. Two years from now, your 12 GB card — thanks to Q3 quantization and MoE architecture — may run what today is a 30B model’s capability.
Three Pieces of Advice for Ordinary Users 12 GB VRAM + 32 GB RAM + 1 TB SSD today is enough for two years. Don’t panic, don’t upgrade yet. If you do upgrade, add RAM and storage before the GPU. Going from 16 GB to 32 GB RAM improves the experience more than going from 12 GB to 16 GB VRAM. Watch quantization and MoE architectures. These two trends directly determine how many more years your current GPU will last. The hardware war for local AI doesn’t refresh like a phone every year. Your 12 GB VRAM has at least two more years of battle left in it.
summary:
My RTX 4070 SUPER 12G runs qwen2.5:14b at Q4 quantization right at the edge of VRAM limits — 9 GB for the model itself, 2 GB for the KV cache, less than 1 GB to spare. That’s the “sweet spot” of 2026. But will this setup still be enough in two years?

This article isn’t about AGI predictions. It’s about one practical question: over the next 1-2 years, how much VRAM, system RAM, and disk will a regular person need to run local LLMs?
title: The Coming War on Memory and Storage: How Much VRAM, RAM, and Disk Will You Need in the Next Two Years?

Deploying Ollama locally seems like a straightforward process, but there are three unexpected issues you might encounter. Here’s a record of them.
Pit 1: Direct Download from Official Website Fails Symptoms: Accessing https://ollama.com/download/OllamaSetup.exe results in PowerShell errors such as Could not resolve host: github.com or Unable to connect to remote server.
Cause: The Ollama official website is just a redirect page, and the actual installation package is hosted on GitHub Releases. Accessing GitHub from domestic networks is unstable and unreliable.
Solution:
First, get the latest version number from https://api.github.com/repos/ollama/ollama/releases/latest. Add a mirror prefix to the GitHub download link, for example: https://ghproxy.net/https://github.com/ollama/ollama/releases/download/vX.Y.Z/OllamaSetup.exe Use curl or a browser to download the file and verify its size (Ollama installation package is approximately 1.4GB). Pit 2: Default Listening Only on 127.0.0.1, Unreachable from Other Devices Symptoms: Ollama runs successfully, but http://192.168.x.x:11434/api/tags cannot be accessed from other devices, while curl http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags works fine on the local machine.
Cause: By default, Ollama sets OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1 for security reasons, which does not expose the service to the local network.
Solution (Run as Administrator in PowerShell):
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OLLAMA_HOST','0.0.0.0','User') Then, restart the Ollama service for the changes to take effect. In Task Manager, end all ollama.exe processes and restart the Ollama application.
Use netstat -ano | findstr 11434 to confirm that the listening address has changed to 0.0.0.0:11434.
Pit 3: Environment Variable Set but Not Read by Service Symptoms: After setting OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0, Ollama still listens on 127.0.0.1 after a restart.
Cause: The Ollama Windows version is a tray application (ollama app.exe), and it starts with the environment variables set at login time. After modifying the user-level environment variable, the tray application must be completely closed (right-click the tray icon → Quit) and restarted. Only restarting the command line ollama serve inherits the current shell environment, but the tray application does not.
Solution:
Check Task Manager to ensure there are no lingering ollama.exe processes. Restart Ollama from the Start Menu. Use netstat to verify. Pit 4: Windows Firewall Blocks External Access Symptoms: The local machine can access http://192.168.x.x:11434, but mobile devices cannot.
Cause: The Windows Defender Firewall blocks external inbound connections to port 11434 by default.
Solution (Run as Administrator in PowerShell):
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Ollama" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 11434 -Protocol TCP -Action Allow To open only to the local network for security:
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Ollama LAN" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 11434 -Protocol TCP -RemoteAddress 192.168.0.0/16 -Action Allow Summary The four issues are not bugs in Ollama itself but rather common obstacles when exposing a local service to the network on Windows. Follow this sequence: use a mirror for downloading → change OLLAMA_HOST → completely restart → allow firewall rules. Once you’ve encountered these issues, you can resolve them in about 10 minutes next time.
summary:
Deploying Ollama locally seems like a straightforward process, but there are three unexpected issues you might encounter. Here’s a record of them.

Pit 1: Direct Download from Official Website Fails

Symptoms: Accessing https://ollama.com/download/OllamaSetup.exe results in PowerShell errors such as Could not resolve host: github.com or Unable to connect to remote server.

Cause: The Ollama official website is just a redirect page, and the actual installation package is hosted on GitHub Releases. Accessing GitHub from domestic networks is unstable and unreliable.
title: Windows Deployment of Ollama Troubleshooting: GitHub Download Failure, Local Network Access, OLLAMA_HOST

Deploying Ollama and setting it up to auto-start on Windows can greatly enhance daily use. However, using the default command-line method may result in a black window popping up at each boot, affecting aesthetics and user experience. This article will provide a detailed guide on how to set up Ollama to auto-start on Windows without displaying a black window, ideal for users needing Ollama to run continuously.
Installing Ollama First, you need to install Ollama on your Windows system. Visit the Ollama official website or related resource pages to download the appropriate installation package for Windows. Follow the official documentation to complete the installation steps, ensuring that Ollama is correctly installed.
Preparing the Run Script To avoid the black window, we need to prepare a run script. Create a new text file named run_ollama.bat, and add the following content:
@echo off start /b "" "C:\Path\To\Ollama.exe" Make sure to replace C:\Path\To\Ollama.exe with the actual path to the Ollama executable file. The start /b parameter is used to start the program in the background without displaying the command prompt window.
Creating a Windows Service Next, we need to use the sc command to create a Windows service to manage Ollama’s startup. Open the command prompt and enter the following command:
sc create OllamaService binPath= "C:\Path\To\run_ollama.bat" Ensure that C:\Path\To\run_ollama.bat is replaced with the actual path to the run script. After creating the service, you can use the following command to set it to auto-start:
sc config OllamaService start= auto Verification and Testing After completing the above steps, restart your computer and check if Ollama auto-starts without displaying a black window. If everything is set up correctly, you should see Ollama running in the background.
Configuration Optimization For further optimization, consider using Task Scheduler to periodically check if Ollama is running normally and automatically restart it if the process does not exist. Create a new task with the trigger set to “At startup” and the action set to start the Ollama run script.
<Triggers> <BootTrigger /> </Triggers> <Actions> <Exec> <Command>C:\Path\To\run_ollama.bat</Command> </Exec> </Actions> Conclusion By following the above steps, you can set up Ollama to auto-start on Windows without displaying a black window, ensuring continuous and stable operation while enhancing the system’s aesthetics and user experience. I hope this article is helpful to you.

Problem How much context can a 12GB VRAM handle when running a 14B model? This is one of the most critical questions when deploying large models locally. This article answers it with real data.
Test Environment GPU: RTX 4070 SUPER (12GB) Model: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Q4_K_M quantization, weights around 9GB Inference Engine: Ollama 0.34 Monitoring Command: ollama ps Practical Measurements Context Length (num_ctx) Model Usage GPU/CPU Ratio Inference Speed 4096 9.5 GB 100% GPU ~49 tok/s 16384 ~11 GB 100% GPU (critical) ~40 tok/s 32768 ~15 GB 34% CPU + 66% GPU ~15-20 tok/s 65536 VRAM overflow Mostly CPU Unavailable Principles The weights of a 14B Q4 model are around 9GB. The remaining 3GB VRAM must accommodate:
KV cache: Approximately hundreds of MB per 1K token context (depends on model layers and hidden dimensions) Activation values and temporary buffers The longer the context, the larger the KV cache. Once VRAM capacity is exceeded, Ollama automatically moves some layers to system memory, exchanging data via PCIe, which is why the speed drops significantly.
Practical Recommendations Use 4096-8192 context for daily conversations: Sufficient for most chat scenarios, and the fastest. Use 16384 for long document analysis: Critical value for 12GB VRAM, still runs full GPU. Use 32768 for code/Agent: Accept the speed penalty of CPU hybrid if necessary. Avoid blindly setting 128K: Qwen2.5 natively supports 128K context, but that requires tens of GB VRAM. How to Adjust Context Length Controlled via the num_ctx parameter in Ollama. Configure in OpenClaw:
{ "params": { "num_ctx": 16384, "keep_alive": "15m" } } Or set directly in Ollama’s Modelfile.
Conclusion The sweet spot for running a 14B model with 12GB VRAM is 8K-16K context. For longer contexts, either upgrade to larger VRAM (24GB+), or accept the speed trade-off of CPU hybrid. Larger models aren’t always better; the right size is key.

What is OpenClaw OpenClaw is an open-source AI Agent Gateway that runs on your own machine, connecting chat channels (Telegram, Discord, Lark, Web UI, etc.) to large models. It is licensed under MIT and has over 100,000 stars on GitHub.
Its value lies in: you send a message, it calls the model, executes tools, maintains sessions, and retains memory—essentially, it upgrades “ollama in the command line” into a truly functional assistant.
System Requirements Node.js ≥ 24.16 (Note: Node 22 LTS is insufficient and will be rejected by the preinstall script) Windows 10/11 A local or remote Ollama instance Installation Steps 1. Install Node.js 24 Download the Windows zip version from nodejs.org, extract it to C:\nodejs, and add it to the user PATH.
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', "$env:Path;C:\nodejs", 'User') 2. Install OpenClaw Globally npm install -g openclaw@latest Pitfall 1: npm 11 introduces a allow-scripts security mechanism that defaults to skipping postinstall scripts for native modules like koffi. You must execute:
npm install -g --allow-scripts=openclaw,@google/genai,koffi,tree-sitter-bash,protobufjs openclaw@latest Otherwise, the startup will fail due to missing native bindings.
3. Configure Local Ollama Edit C:\Users\<you>\.openclaw\openclaw.json:
{ "gateway": { "mode": "local" }, "models": { "providers": { "ollama": { "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:11434", "models": [ { "id": "qwen2.5:14b", "contextWindow": 32768, "params": { "num_ctx": 32768, "keep_alive": "15m" } } ] } } }, "agents": { "defaults": { "model": { "primary": "ollama/qwen2.5:14b" } } } } Pitfall 2: The OpenClaw Ollama provider must use the native API (baseUrl without /v1). Using the OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint will cause tool calls to fail.
Pitfall 3: Not writing the API key in the configuration file is not enough—it exists in the local SQLite authentication database. The first run requires:
"ollama-local" | openclaw models auth paste-api-key --provider ollama 4. Start the Gateway openclaw gateway install # Install to start on boot openclaw gateway restart Open your browser and visit http://127.0.0.1:18789/, log in with the token output by openclaw gateway auth-token --show, and you can chat in the Web UI.
Performance Test With qwen2.5:14b as the backend, on a machine with 12GB of VRAM:
Normal conversations run 100% on GPU, approximately 49 tok/s Long context (32K) will partially spill over to memory, reducing speed Agent mode (with tool calls) is fully functional, but the 14B model’s understanding of complex multi-step toolchains is inferior to that of GPT-4-level models Conclusion OpenClaw is currently the most straightforward solution for turning local models into “real assistants”. The deployment process is more challenging than expected (Node version, npm security mechanisms, context window size issues), but once set up, it becomes a fully functional, self-starting local agent that can be accessed via Web UI and connected to Telegram/Lark.
summary:
What is OpenClaw

OpenClaw is an open-source AI Agent Gateway that runs on your own machine, connecting chat channels (Telegram, Discord, Lark, Web UI, etc.) to large models. It is licensed under MIT and has over 100,000 stars on GitHub.

Its value lies in: you send a message, it calls the model, executes tools, maintains sessions, and retains memory—essentially, it upgrades “ollama in the command line” into a truly functional assistant.
title: Deploying OpenClaw in Practice: Setting Up a Personal AI Assistant with Local Large Models

Step 1: Install Ollama Download the Windows installer from ollama.com/download and run it silently by double-clicking.
Troubleshooting Tip: The official website hosts the installer on GitHub Releases. If you are in China and direct access fails with “Could not resolve host: github.com”, use a GitHub mirror (such as ghproxy) to retry.
After installation, open cmd to verify:
ollama --version Step 2: Pull the Model ollama pull qwen2.5:14b The model is approximately 9GB, and the download speed depends on your network. Confirm the download with ollama list.
Step 3: Validate Inference ollama run qwen2.5:14b Enter a sentence directly to test. The first inference will load the model into VRAM, taking about 10-20 seconds.
Step 4: Open Local Network Access (Optional) By default, Ollama only listens on 127.0.0.1:11434, which is not accessible from other devices. Set the environment variable and restart:
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('OLLAMA_HOST','0.0.0.0','User','User') After restarting the Ollama service, local network devices can access the API via http://<your LAN IP>:11434.
VRAM Usage Testing Context Length GPU Usage Speed 4096 100% GPU ~49 tok/s 32768 34% CPU + 66% GPU Significantly slower With 12GB VRAM, the KV cache space is limited after loading 14B Q4. Longer contexts will overflow to memory, reducing speed. 4K context is sufficient for daily conversations.
Final Thoughts Running a 14B model locally is not about being “better than GPT-4”, but about: no data leaving the machine, no API fees, offline use, and customizable settings. If you have a card with more than 12GB VRAM, this step is worth taking.
